children: By Mark R. Long

The closure of the Strait of Hormuz has DP World racing to reroute cargo around a bottleneck that once seemed improbable. Trade at the Port of Jebel Ali, the crown jewel of DP World's global network, plummeted 90%, posing a challenge to Yuvraj Narayan, the new CEO of the Middle East's largest port operator.

Jebel Ali serves as a gateway to the Middle East as well as a transshipment hub connecting Asia, Europe, the Americas and Africa. To keep food and other essential commodities flowing to Dubai, DP World is shifting cargoes to road and rail networks linked to ports in the Gulf of Oman, the Red Sea and as far away as Turkey. The company has also added 700 trucks to its Middle East fleet and committed $500 million to build two new port facilities on the Gulf of Oman to bypass Hormuz.

Narayan took charge of DP World in mid-February. A DP World veteran who previously served as CFO and deputy CEO, he tells the WSJ Logistics Report's Paul Berger about mounting losses at Jebel Ali and whether the port can recover as a crossroads for global trade.

Manufacturing & Energy

A California startup called Parallax is using 3-D printing technology to help make a key piece of equipment for data centers: gas turbines. The Wall Street Journal's Jennifer Hiller writes that Parallax has raised $117 million to enter the market for smaller, gas-fired turbines for on-site power, using 3-D printing instead of the specialty supply chain for turbines.

The market for large turbines used at power plants has multiyear backlogs because of rising demand for power, much of it coming from the AI boom. Many data centers are deciding to go it alone and build their own power generation on site.

Parallax founder and CEO Carl Schoeller said the idea isn't to attempt to replicate the highly efficient turbines that major manufacturers build. Instead, he wants to make something smaller that could generate about 10 megawatts of electricity, be manufactured faster with cheaper materials and be transported in shipping containers.
Number of the Day
Additional square miles required to produce enough biofuels for nations to meet all their targets for blending them into gasoline and diesel, according to Chatham House.
Automation
Amazon said it would spend more than $100 million on a new robotics factory near Indianapolis as it automates more of the work inside its warehouses.

The WSJ's Isabella Simonetti writes that (Amazon), already one of the world's biggest robot makers, last month announced plans to construct another robotics hub in Austin, Texas. The new facilities will double the number of Amazon's robot-making plants to four.

Amazon's investments in robotics, which date to its $775 million acquisition of Kiva Systems in 2012, have put it at the center of a debate around how automation and AI will affect workers, including its own workforce of more than 1.5 million. The company says its investments in robots to sort, lift and move packages have created high-paying, skilled jobs and reduced the rate of recordable workplace injuries by more than 40%.
